Cournot competition is QUANTITY competition: each firm chooses its output $q_i$, taking rivals’ outputs as given, and the market price comes from total quantity $Q=\sum_i q_i$ via the inverse demand $P(Q)$.

Firm $i$ solves

$$
\max_{q_i \ge 0}\ \pi_i(q_i,q_{-i}) = P(q_i+q_{-i})q_i - C_i(q_i)
$$

so the key condition is $MR_i=MC_i$, where

$$
MR_i = \frac{d}{dq_i}\left[P(Q)q_i\right] = P(Q) + q_i P'(Q).
$$

That FOC gives a best response function $q_i = BR_i(q_{-i})$; a Cournot Nash equilibrium is where the firms’ best responses intersect (each output is a best response to the other).

“Omitted variable bias” means: if the true model has a relevant variable $X_2$ but you leave it out and regress $Y$ only on $X_1$, your estimated slope on $X_1$ picks up some of $X_2$’s effect.

Write the true model as

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1 X_{1i}+\beta_2 X_{2i}+e_i
$$

If you omit $X_2$, the regression error becomes

$$
u_i=\beta_2 X_{2i}+e_i
$$

So if $X_1$ and $X_2$ move together, then $X_1$ is correlated with the error term, and OLS no longer targets $\beta_1$. In the course materials, the probability limit is

$$
\operatorname{plim}(\hat\beta_1)=\beta_1+\beta_2\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)}{\operatorname{Var}(X_1)}
$$

No bias happens if either $\beta_2=0$ (the omitted variable doesn’t affect $Y$) or $\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=0$ (it’s unrelated to $X_1$).

In your own words, what’s the $X_2$ you’re worried is being left out, and do you think it’s positively or negatively related to $X_1$?

A p-value is:

$$p = P(\text{getting a test statistic at least this extreme} \mid H_0 \text{ is true})$$

So you temporarily assume the null hypothesis $H_0$ is true, and then ask: “How surprising is my sample result under that assumption?” Smaller p-value means your result would be rare if $H_0$ were true.

Key NON-meaning (from the course materials): the p-value is NOT

$$P(H_0 \text{ is true} \mid \text{the data})$$

Which direction “at least this extreme” goes depends on the alternative hypothesis ($H_A$): two-sided means extreme in either direction; one-sided means only one tail.

The “last step” is forming the test statistic as

$$
t=\frac{\text{estimate}-\text{null value}}{SE(\text{estimate})}.
$$

In a regression table, the estimate is the coefficient $\hat\beta$ and the null value is usually $0$, so

$$
t=\frac{\hat\beta-0}{SE(\hat\beta)}=\frac{\hat\beta}{SE(\hat\beta)}.
$$

In a one-sample mean test, the estimate is $\bar y$ and the null value is $\mu_0$, so

$$
t=\frac{\bar y-\mu_0}{SE(\bar y)}.
$$

Which case are you in (regression coefficient, one-sample mean, or difference in two means), and what are your estimate and standard error?

You subtract the mean because variance is defined as “how far values are from the center,” and the center is $E[X]$ (or the sample mean $\bar X$). Formally,

$$\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[(X-E[X])^2]$$

Squaring does two jobs: it prevents positive and negative deviations from canceling out, and it makes large deviations count more. In a sample, you divide by $n-1$ (instead of $n$) because once you’ve used the data to estimate $\bar X$, the deviations $(X_i-\bar X)$ have one constraint (they sum to 0), so $n-1$ gives an unbiased estimate of the population variance.

Are you computing a SAMPLE variance $s^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar X)^2$ or a population variance $\sigma^2=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\mu)^2$?

Heteroskedasticity means the spread of the regression errors changes with $X$.

In the ideal “constant variance” case (homoskedasticity), you assume

$$
\text{Var}(u \mid x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\sigma^2
$$

With heteroskedasticity, that variance depends on $X$ instead of being constant, so points might be tightly clustered for low $X$ but very spread out for high $X$ (a “fan shape” in a residual plot). OLS coefficient estimates can still be unbiased/consistent under the usual exogeneity assumption, but the usual OLS standard errors are wrong, so $t$ tests, $F$ tests, and confidence intervals become unreliable. The standard fix is to use heteroskedasticity-robust (Huber-White) standard errors; other fixes include transforming variables or using weighted least squares if you can model the variance.

Structural unemployment is when people want to work but their skills, location, or experience don’t match the jobs that are actually available.

It often comes from changes in the economy like new technology, industries shrinking or growing, or consumers shifting what they buy (for example, fewer manufacturing jobs and more service-sector jobs).

It tends to last longer than frictional unemployment because workers may need time to retrain, get new credentials, or relocate.

Vertical integration means one firm owns or tightly controls multiple stages of the same value chain, typically an upstream stage (inputs/manufacturing) and a downstream stage (distribution/retail). For example, instead of a manufacturer selling to an independent retailer, a single integrated retailer-manufacturer makes the product and sells it to consumers itself.

A core reason firms do this in this course is to eliminate DOUBLE MARGINALIZATION: when the manufacturer and retailer each add their own markup, the final price can end up too high and total profit (combined) can be lower than what an integrated firm would choose. Vertical integration can also improve coordination (inventory, quality, service levels), but it can create antitrust concerns if it forecloses rivals’ access to key inputs or customers.

Example: two coffee shops on a straight street (Hotelling).

Consumers are located at $x \in [0,1]$, Firm 1 at $x_1=0$, Firm 2 at $x_2=1$. A consumer at $x$ gets utility from buying from firm $i$:

$$
U_i(x)= v - p_i - t|x-x_i|
$$

Here, $t$ is the “transportation cost” (how painful it is to buy the less convenient option). If $t$ is large, lots of consumers are effectively “captive” to the closer shop, so each shop can raise price without losing many customers, meaning price competition is softer than if the shops sold an identical product in the same location.

Coopetition means two firms are RIVALS in some areas but PARTNERS in others at the same time.

Rephrased: they compete to win customers, but they cooperate where it benefits both (like sharing a technology standard, co-developing a component, or using the same distribution network).

Example: two smartphone makers compete on finished phones, but collaborate on a shared charging standard or jointly source key parts to reduce costs.

The course materials don’t use the term explicitly, but you can think of it as a strategic choice about WHICH parts of the “game” are competitive and which parts are cooperative.

where $\bar x_g$ and $s_g$ are the sample mean and sample SD in group $g\in\{W,A\}$, and $n_g$ is the group size.

In R, one clean way is:
